Quasi-legislative hearings, by contrast, bear a greater resemblance to 
congressional committee hearings. They are essentially unregulated by due 
process and are held for the purpose of allowing those who may be affected 
by a proposed rule to air their views and help to inform the agency s 
legislative judgment. Although a record of a legislative-type hearing 
typically is made, the final decision (i.e., the rule) may be based on 
considerations that come from outside the hearing record. Indeed, the most 
important input—the agency’s legislative or expert judgment—may be 
uTeducible to the record.
Third, whether an APA hearing is required depends on the complex 
interplay between the APA and the agencies’ organic statutes. The APA’s 
hearing provisions apply only when some other statute—that is, the statute 
that an agency is implementing—^requires a decision “to be determined on 
the record after opportunity for an agency hearing.” 5 U.S.C. §§ 553(c), 
554(a). The procedures described chiefly in 5 U.S.C. sections 556 and 557 
are apphcable in “formal” rulemaking and in “formal” adjudication, 
respectively. In other words, they supply minimum procedures for judicial-
type hearings and not for legislative-type hearings. Although these APA 
sections raise their own issues of interpretation, it is easy enough to 
confirm their applicability when another statute refers to them expressly 
or incorporates the precise triggering language just quoted. Often, 
however, an agency statute requires a “hearing” or “public hearing,” but 
fails to say whether this amounts to a requirement that decisions ‘Td o 
determined on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing.” Indeed, 
as explained in the preceding paragraph, the APA’s “on the record” 
language refers to a concept that was developed in pre-APA due process 
caselaw, rather than to any pre-APA statutory drafting convention.
Fourth, Congress may confer a right to a hearing in language that 
would trigger the APA but specify, in the same statute, different or 
additional procedures. In such a circumstance, the APA does not provide a 
comprehensive guide to the applicable procedural requirements, but 
instead supphes a backdrop that fills in the procedural details that 
Congress did not specifically cover. In some cases, these statutes may 
entirely displace the APA, despite § 559’s instruction that “subsequent 
statute may not be held to supersede or modify” the APA “except to the 
extent that it does so expressly.’^ See, e.g., Marcello v. Bonds, 349 U.S. 302 
(1955) (interpreting procedural provisions in the Immigration and 
Naturahzation Act of 1952 to displace the APA’s hearing requirements in 
deportation proceedings).
